sections.section_title: The New Heaven, New Earth, and the Descending City
sections.summary: The seer witnesses the appearance of a new heaven and new earth after the passing away of the first creation and the sea; the holy city, new Jerusalem, descends from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband, fulfilling the promise to the overcomer at Philadelphia (3:12) and identifying the city with the bride community whose righteous acts constitute her garments (19:7-8).

A voice from the throne declares the theological center of the new creation -- God's tabernacle is with humanity, the covenant formula ('they shall be his people, and God himself will be among them') is fulfilled in its ultimate form, and the consequences of the old order (tears, death, mourning, crying, pain) are comprehensively abolished, completing the promise of 7:17 and fulfilling Isaiah 25:8.

sections.section_title: The Declaration from the Throne -- Making All Things New
sections.summary: God speaks directly from the throne, declaring 'I am making all things new,' authenticating the words as 'faithful and true,' announcing 'It is done,' identifying himself as the Alpha and Omega, offering the water of life freely to the thirsty, promising that the overcomer will inherit all things and become God's son, and warning that the cowardly, unbelieving, abominable, murderers, immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and liars face the second death.
sections.relevance: This passage directly addresses salvation outcomes -- inheriting the new creation versus facing the second death -- and presents them as contingent on human choices. The overcomer (ho nikon) inherits; the coward and the faithless face the lake of fire. The neutral reading explicitly identifies the cowardly (deiloi) not as people who experience fear but as those 'whose fear causes them to abandon their allegiance' -- capitulation under the beast's demands is a volitional act. The faithless (apistoi) are 'those who do not keep faith, who abandon trust under pressure' -- again, a choice. The invitation to 'the one who thirsts' (to dipsOnti) echoes Isaiah 55:1's open invitation requiring human initiative (coming, taking), and the water is offered 'without cost' (dOrean), paralleling Revelation 22:17 ('let the one who is thirsty come; let the one who desires take'). The neutral reading concludes: 'The choice placed before the assemblies in chapters 2-3 -- to overcome or to capitulate -- finds its eternal consequences here.' God speaks from the throne and the content of his speech is an invitation requiring response and a warning presupposing genuine alternatives. The passage is not an aside or illustration but God's own direct declaration of the two paths and their outcomes, making it a first-order statement about human agency in salvation.
key_phrases: I will give to the one who thirsts from the spring of the water of life without cost
He who overcomes will inherit these things, and I will be his God and he will be my son
But for the cowardly and unbelieving... their part will be in the lake that burns with fire and brimstone, which is the second death
the choice placed before the assemblies... to overcome or to capitulate... finds its eternal consequences here

sections.section_title: The Angel Shows the Bride -- The City's Identity and Structure
sections.summary: One of the seven bowl-angels -- in deliberate structural mirror of the harlot-showing in 17:1 -- invites John to see the bride, the wife of the Lamb; John is carried in the Spirit to a great and high mountain and shown the holy city with God's glory, its jasper brilliance, its twelve gates inscribed with the twelve tribes' names, its twelve foundations inscribed with the twelve apostles' names, and its four-directional accessibility declaring universal welcome.

An angel measures the city with a golden rod, revealing its dimensions as a perfect cube of twelve thousand stadia per side -- the shape of the Holy of Holies -- with a wall of 144 cubits (12 x 12), every measurement encoding the covenant number twelve and its multiples to convey theological comprehensiveness rather than architectural specification.

The city is constructed of jasper walls, transparent gold, twelve precious foundation stones recalling the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28) and Isaiah's jeweled Jerusalem (Isaiah 54:11-12), pearl gates contrasting the harlot's exploitative pearl-adornment (17:4; 18:12), and a main street of transparent gold -- materials that transmit rather than block God's glory.

sections.section_title: No Temple, No Sun -- God and the Lamb as Temple and Light
sections.summary: The new Jerusalem has no temple because God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple -- the mediating structure is replaced by unmediated divine presence -- and no sun or moon because God's glory illuminates the city and the Lamb is its lamp, fulfilling Isaiah 60:19-20 and completing the pattern of removing every intermediary between God and his people.

sections.section_title: The Nations, the Open Gates, and the Exclusion of the Unclean
sections.summary: The nations walk by the city's light and the kings of the earth bring their glory into it, fulfilling Isaiah 60:3; the gates are permanently open because no night or threat exists; the glory and honor of the nations flow into the city; nothing unclean, no practitioner of abomination or falsehood enters; and entry belongs exclusively to those written in the Lamb's book of life.
sections.relevance: The passage presents two simultaneous criteria governing who belongs in the new Jerusalem: behavioral exclusion (nothing unclean, no one who practices abomination or lying) and positive inscription in the Lamb's book of life. The behavioral criteria presuppose genuine human agency -- the excluded are identified by what they practice (poiOn bdelygma kai pseudos), implying real choices that determine their standing. The gates are permanently open (ou me kleisthOsin, the strongest Greek negation), declaring that access is perpetually available rather than sealed by divine decree. The nations and kings come willingly, bringing their glory -- a picture of voluntary submission, not compelled inclusion. The book of life introduces the Lamb's agency: it is 'his possession, his record, his determination of who belongs to his community,' connected to 'his death and resurrection (5:6, 9) which constituted the purchase of the people whose names are recorded.' However, as established in the document's own logic (3:5, where the overcomer's name will not be blotted out), the book is responsive to faithfulness rather than a fixed predetermining register. The passage leans libertarian because the dominant features -- open gates, universal accessibility from all four directions, behavioral criteria for exclusion, nations voluntarily streaming in -- all emphasize availability and human response, while the book of life functions within a documentary context where it responds to human faithfulness.
key_phrases: the nations will walk by its light
its gates will never be shut
nothing unclean, and no one who practices abomination and lying, shall ever come into it
but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life
